newsitem.title: USA: New England Elec $1.675 bln sale cuts 1,600 jobs.
newsitem.headline: New England Elec $1.675 bln sale cuts 1,600 jobs.

text.p: The $1.675 billion sale of New England Electric System's non-nuclear generating business totalling more than 5,000 megawats of power is expected to result in 1,600 jobs lost, the head of the company said Wednesday.

Asked how many of the 4,800 workers would be cut as a result of the sale of 18 plants to U.S. Generating Co, an affiliate of PG&E Corp, NES chief executive officer John Rowe said, "We believe that when this transaction is consumated, we will need something on the order of 3,200 workers in the retail business. That's a 1,600 employee difference."
Rowe said he did not know how many of those workers U.S. Generating would keep, "but we're assuming 50 percent."

U.S. Generating CEO P. Crisman Iribe said, "Our parent company has had considerable success...working in a partnership with unions. These facilities are heading into a competitive environment and cost and cost control is extremely important."

The agreement for $1.59 billion cash, plus $85 million for employee severance and retirement packages, covering 15 hyrdoplants and three fossil fuel plants that Rowe said are mostly coal fire units, puts pressure on the Massachusetts Legislature to quickly approve the customer choice option.

The deal calls for $225 million to be paid when the customer choice power option is available to either 50 percent of New England ratepayers or 89 percent of Massachusetts ratepayers, Rowe said. If the Massachusetts Legislature fails to approve the option next year, neither goal will be reached.
The money is meant "as protection for U.S. Gen.," he said.

He estimated that if the regulatory and legislative hurdles are met, NEES's 1.3 million ratepayers will see the price for electricity drop between 15 and 18 percent from 2.8 cents a kilowatt hour to its 2.0 cents and "if it opens fast enough 1.6 cents a kilowatt hour."
The book value of the assets was $1.1 billion and the $500 million to $600 million paid over book will retire nearly all of the NEES's fossil, hydro and nuclear power stranded costs, Rowe said.
It will leave NEES with $900 million of power purchase obligations, nuclear decommissioning costs and regulatory assets.
In anticipation of receipt of the proceeds from the sale, NEES's board authorized the repurchase of up to 5 million of its common shares.

U.S. Generating's Iribe said the deal, expected to take up to 18 months to be consumated, would be financed "will a direct infusion of capital from Pacific (PG&E) with some borrowings against U.S. Gen's other plants."
At least one Wall Street analyst liked the deal. HSBC James Capel raised his rating on NEES to buy from hold, analyst Daniel Ford said in a research note.
Ford upgraded the NEES's 12-month share price target to $41 and raised the 1998 earnings per share forecast to $3.24 from $3.05.
